h1: BMC wrote the evaluation criteria buyers were missing
sub: A buyer’s guide comparing Control-M to named rivals, built in the structure AI assistants cite
problem_h2: The shortlist was set before sales arrived
problem_paras: In enterprise software the buyer does the research now. Orchestration is bought by groups, and each member forms a view before anyone talks to sales. By the time a workflow orchestration buyer spoke to a salesperson, the shortlist was usually already decided, and Control-M had no voice in any of it.

Search engines, AI assistants, competitor content and review-site signals were shaping the comparison criteria. The category was moving from job scheduling to workflow orchestration, and many buyers were still searching for the older, simpler tool for a problem that had become far more complex. Buyers at the consideration stage were calibrating what good enough looked like, and which platforms to shortlist. So the insight was straightforward. The team that controls the evaluation criteria controls the shortlist. The leap was to build a guide that does not sell.
solution_intro_paras: The buyer’s guide to workflow orchestration laid out seven critical capabilities, then compared Control-M, RunMyJobs and Stonebranch side by side, in the shape a buyer would build in a spreadsheet. One artifact powered the whole consideration journey, running through the landing page, paid search, content syndication, account-based media and review sites.

acc_items.title: Designed to be cited
acc_items.body: Buyers had started asking AI assistants how to evaluate orchestration platforms. Structured comparison and explicit criteria-and-trade-off framing are the shapes large language models and search engines cite, so the guide was engineered to be that source.

acc_items.title: Three named account lists

Windows 10 was nearing end-of-support, leaving 24M+ commercial devices ineligible for upgrade, and pandemic-era PCs were aging out. The window would not stay open. Partner interviews revealed that most leads were sitting dormant, and not for lack of interest. No one had time to qualify them. Partners didn’t need more names, they needed someone to verify contacts and route the right leads to sales. With BDR hiring off the table, HP built its own.
solution_h2: An AI agent built for outcomes
solution_intro_paras: HP built an AI sales agent powered by Claude’s latest language models and integrated with workflow automations. acc_items.title: Signals layered over partner profiles
acc_items.body: Partners supplied ideal customer profiles. An AI model was trained to look beyond firmographics, using signals like tech stack maturity and hiring velocity to identify similar accounts. The agent then ran outreach across those targets.

acc_items.title: Onboarded like a junior BDR
acc_items.body: Execution began with a clear, compliant conversation flow. Each call opened with AI disclosure and followed a logic tree built to guide the interaction. A central knowledge base held HP product information and partner context.

acc_items.title: Content at scale, powered by AI
acc_items.body: Instead of building from scratch, HP’s content library was audited for reuse potential. A model trained on HP’s editorial standards and segmentation insights refreshed 20 assets in under two weeks, some of them two to three years old.

h1: Microsoft gives resellers a showcase kit for the full Surface line-up

problem_h2: The benefit and curse of premium
problem_paras: In the competitive commercial tech space, Surface devices were premium offerings whose high price point demanded an in-person experience for buyers to appreciate their value. Commercial devices are bought through reseller partners, and with a portfolio of over 10 devices, showing the full line-up was getting harder.

Partner success is Microsoft’s success. The strategy was partner-centric, aimed at resellers who drive Surface device sales and build brand equity with customers. Microsoft wanted a modern demo kit partners could use for engaging device demos, and budgets were tight enough that partners would pay for the kit themselves. Knowing it was a tall order, Microsoft expected to sell 20. In a risky move, almost all the money went into designing and producing the kits, on the hope that its creativity would sell itself.
solution_intro_paras: The first-ever Hybrid Device Showcase Kit worked in both realms. A sleek and sturdy travelling case held up to 6 devices and essential accessories, so partners could transport Surface devices and do demos on the go. A digital version supported follow-up conversations and self-guided virtual demos.

acc_items.title: A case built to travel
acc_items.body: The interior was custom-fitted to hold Surface devices and accessories securely. The design struck a balance between ruggedness and refinement. There was even room for a table skirt if partners were headed to a trade show.

acc_items.title: The full line-up, from anywhere
acc_items.body: Partners activated the digital version when customers could not meet in person. It offered an immersive virtual environment where customers could explore the full Surface lineup, picking a device and looking at it from every angle.

acc_items.title: A premium look, rendered in 3D

acc_items.title: Numbers built into the demo

h1: Microsoft trains Teams users with the most dysfunctional office ever

problem_h2: A race for the meeting platform
problem_paras: March 2020 started a race for who would become the leading productivity and meeting platform for remote work. Most companies had not picked a unified meeting solution. Hundreds of thousands of users had access to Microsoft Teams but simply weren’t using it.

Video and webinar fatigue was setting in for remote workers. To deal with it all, people were binge-watching their favourite shows. The most popular show of 2020 was “The Office.” Simply walking people through Teams features was not going to win anyone over. So the answer was to use the most dysfunctional office environment ever to teach people how to use world-class productivity tools. If people got comfortable using Teams, it would become embedded in their new daily routine.
solution_intro_paras: The (Modern) Office was a virtual training session opened by Todd Packer, who explained how Microsoft Teams would have made life better at Dunder Mifflin. After the laughs came a guided walk-through of Teams, covering group chats and project timelines.

acc_items.title: Characters joined as Teams members
acc_items.body: The concept went beyond Todd’s appearance. As Michael Scott and Jim Halpert joined as members in Teams, the demo illustrated creating group chats, participating in video calls, managing workback schedules, and sending GIFs.

acc_items.title: One call to action per session
acc_items.body: The engagement and excitement created in each session was channelled toward a single action. At the end of every session, viewers were called out to request training for their departments, to achieve the scale and impact needed.

acc_items.title: Equipping the sales teams
acc_items.body: Given the account-based focus, Microsoft sales teams were engaged as demand gen champions. They were equipped with a complete bill of materials including collateral, social selling copy decks, email signatures, and email templates.

acc_items.title: An account-based route to scale
acc_items.body: The opportunity was clearest in strategic accounts already using Teams but not using its meeting features. Sales teams used the novel experience to bring some much-needed laughter to their customers’ days.

h1: SAP replaces traditional video production with photorealistic AI avatars
sub: Studio-quality multilingual avatars, a global playbook, a structured intake form and a centralized tracker
problem_h2: Video production without a shared system
problem_paras: SAP powers over two-thirds of the world’s transactions, and that scale demands constant communication across regions and industries. Product teams were producing their own videos, with overlapping content and no shared system. An audit found three video formats duplicated across dozens of teams, with inconsistent style and rising costs.

SAP’s marketing team started with the basics. Could content be templated or production batched? Could centralized talent reduce cost and variability? Each adjustment helped on the margins, but none came close to the 25% cost and speed improvements the business needed. The problem was not creative. It was capacity. Traditional workflows, no matter how refined, could not scale to match SAP’s global footprint. Rather than shrink its video footprint, SAP saw a chance to redesign video production entirely.
solution_intro_paras: SAP piloted photorealistic AI avatars as a creative alternative. These were studio-quality, fully multilingual avatars capable of generating content in 140+ languages, instantly and on demand. No studio bookings, no reshoots. If a line was missed, it could be regenerated instantly, even in another language.

acc_items.title: Putting people in the director’s chair
acc_items.body: Internal teams were hesitant to adopt a new system. SAP built a global playbook setting brand and quality standards, a structured intake form to streamline briefs, and a centralized tracker for transparency across teams and regions.

acc_items.title: Built to engage, beat for beat
acc_items.body: Internal benchmarks showed videos with a clear narrative outperformed demos. SAP introduced a five-part story framework running from a proactive opening line and a headline takeaway through a real-world challenge, a guided demo and a recap.

acc_items.title: Bringing the brand into frame
acc_items.body: SAP extended its visual language across every asset. The anvil icon became a design system, appearing in animations and layout patterns. Each video combined avatars, animated interstitials and screen recordings with subtle sound design.

acc_items.title: Earning views while upholding values
acc_items.body: SAP committed to using AI with clarity and care. Every video included an “AI-generated video” disclosure. Avatars were designed to reflect global diversity, so the people in SAP’s stories looked like the people watching them.
